name: PT Bank Rakyat Indonesia (Persero) Tbk

frontmatter.title: BRI: a franchise priced for a broken credit cycle
frontmatter.summary: We keep BBRI at BUY with a twelve-month value of Rp4,010, a 62.0% total return from Rp2,710, dividends included. The shares cost 1.2x forward book for a bank that earned 17.7% on equity in FY2025 and 18.1% in the nine months to September. The third quarter again beat on credit and funding; the argument is whether micro losses stay near their peak.
thesis: Micro is the franchise and the problem: BRI lends where the rest of the system will not, at yields the corporate book cannot match, so losses rather than margins set the return.

Credit cost is the swing factor. We hold it near the top of its observed five-year range through the cycle rather than at the low end of this year's guidance, and that choice accounts for most of the difference between our value and the price.

Capital return is the second lever, and we do not assume it falls. The payout is held at the 92.0% the company actually distributes: the balance sheet funds about 8.0% loan growth through FY2032E and then only the 1.6% that retained capital supports, while the estimated capital ratio holds above the floor. That payout funds only modest perpetual growth, so terminal growth is the 1.6% retention supports rather than a bank-growth rate it cannot finance.

The multiple embeds a perpetual return on equity in the mid-teens, against the high teens the bank reported in each of the last three years and 18.1% in the nine months to September; that gap is the whole investment case.

The peer screen is the main risk to the call: BRI trades above the median large bank and above BMRI despite a lower return and several times the credit cost, so part of the upside needs the sector-wide de-rating to unwind.

blocks.text: Update, 9 November 2026. Nine-month consolidated profit was IDR48.16tn, 16.8% higher year on year, on interest income of IDR162.79tn and a 18.1% return on equity [S14][S15]. Gross NPL 3.1%, net NPL 1.0% and loans at risk 9.5% all improved year on year, and third-party funds grew 12.0% to IDR1,651.00tn with CASA at 70.0% [S14][S15][S8]. This revision rebuilds the capital block on one perimeter - consolidated equity over the risk-weighted assets implied by the consolidated ratio the filings report it against - and corrects the payout and margin labels; the rating and thesis carry forward [S7][S15].

We keep BUY with a twelve-month value of Rp4,010 a share, a total return of 62.0% from the Rp2,710 last traded, of which Rp379 is dividends. Justified price-to-book carries half the weight, residual income three tenths and a dividend discount model the balance: book value and the return earned on it, not growth, are what the price argues about.

At 1.2x forward book the market embeds a perpetual return on equity in the mid-teens against 17.7% in FY2025, 19.1% in FY2024 and 19.7% in FY2023 [S6], and the 19.6% we capitalise at a 12.5% cost of equity. Three things decide the value: credit cost, taken to 3.2% in FY2026E and 3.4% through the cycle between the last two actuals [S4]; a margin that gives up little after an eighty-three basis point fall in loan yield to 12.2%, but which we do not hold flat [S4]; and capital return, with the payout held at the 92.0% actually distributed [S7], which carries the estimated consolidated ratio from 22.0% to 16.4% by FY2032E before loan growth tapers to the 1.6% that retention funds [S4][S15].

Scenarios are weighted 50.0% base, 25.0% bear and 25.0% bull. The bear is an operating downside, not the price: at a credit cost above even the FY2021 stress share the shares are still worth Rp2,874 today and Rp2,956 in twelve months, above the Rp2,710 price, so the target is not produced by the downside; the base is worth Rp4,081 today and drives the 62.0% return. The bull is the nine-month run-rate simply continuing [S14][S15].

We would step back if micro formation re-accelerates while the book shrinks, if double-digit loan growth runs another year at this payout and takes the capital ratio through the floor or forces a raise, or if deposit growth trails the system for two consecutive quarters.

Bank Rakyat Indonesia is the country's largest lender by loan book and the only large bank whose franchise was built on village-level microcredit. At the end of FY2025 it carried gross loans of IDR1,460.73tn and customer deposits of IDR1,466.84tn, a loan-to-deposit ratio of 99.6%, on earning assets of IDR2,029.08tn and equity of IDR324.03tn [S6][S4]. The government holds 53.2% of the shares through Danantara Asset Management, including one Series A Dwiwarna share, and the public holds 46.8% [S3].

The book spans micro, consumer, small and medium enterprise, commercial and corporate segments; micro is both the largest and the source of the margin premium and the credit losses [S4]. Within micro the state-subsidised KUR programme is the growth engine: KUR outstanding reached IDR293.40tn, up 10.2%, while Kupedes fell 20.4% to IDR153.50tn from IDR192.80tn; micro was 43.4% of consolidated loans [S4]. KUR carries a government guarantee and a capped rate, so margin and risk are both lower than in the Kupedes book. The model grows the consolidated LK "Loans" line, IDR1,583.77tn at 30 September against IDR1,460.73tn at the end of 2025, while the 14.5% headline is the wider credit-and-financing measure including sharia [S15][S14].

The income statement needs the same care: the pack's conventional net interest income of IDR136.85tn plus non-interest income of IDR50.03tn excludes the sharia unit's net contribution of IDR14.92tn less IDR1.27tn, insurance service income of IDR1.30tn, net gold revenue of IDR2.40tn and other operating income of IDR53.68tn [S6].

The franchise runs through the largest retail branch and agent network in the country; BRILink and BRImo fund it cheaply, with savings and current accounts growing 10.1% against total deposits of 6.7% and CASA at 67.6% [S4]. The strategy rebuilds micro underwriting rather than abandoning the segment, and system MSME lending grew 2.7% against 13.3% for the system [S8][S4].

BRI began as a savings institution for civil servants in the colonial administration and was repurposed several times before becoming the state vehicle for subsidised microcredit. Its village units and later its agent network gave it a distribution cost base that urban commercial banks could not replicate, which is why the micro segment has stayed profitable for it through cycles that damaged smaller competitors.

System loans grew 13.3% in the year to September, decelerating through the second half as the base effect and tighter liquidity bite, while deposits grew 8.2% - the single most important fact for a lender funded from retail savings rather than wholesale markets [S8]. By use of funds, investment credit grew fastest, working capital ran near average and consumption lagged [S8].

Composition is where BRI's problem lives: corporate credit grew at more than seven times the rate of MSME credit, and state-owned banks grew faster than the system, so the segment BRI dominates is the slowest-growing part of the market and the segments where it is a challenger are the fastest [S8].

BRI's share of system loans was 15.4% at the end of 2025, broadly stable [S3]. Its deposit share slipped through FY2025 and the first half, then reversed: third-quarter third-party funds grew 12.0% to IDR1,651.00tn ahead of the system, with CASA at 70.0% [S14][S8].

BRI leads a segment with the highest yields and the highest loss rates and is a challenger where spreads are thin. Its moat is distribution - an agent and branch footprint that reaches borrowers no urban bank can serve economically, and a deposit franchise built on the same footprint - and it is a cost moat, because the KUR rate is administered and the micro borrower is price-sensitive at the margin [S4]. The five forces are unfavourable at the edges: fintech balance-sheet lenders compete for the same borrowers without the branch cost but also without the deposit base, depositors are more price-sensitive, and substitutes are limited only because the borrower has no collateral and no credit history.

Regulation cuts both ways: the administered KUR rate protects volume but caps revenue per loan, and capital and liquidity rules constrain how fast a systemically important bank can grow risk-weighted assets [S4]. Bank Indonesia cut the conventional reserve requirement to 7.0% from 1 November 2026 [S17], and state ownership through Danantara adds a policy dimension because the shareholder that appoints the board also sets the dividend expectation [S7].

The conclusion is uncomfortable: BRI leads the slowest-growing segment of a double-digit market, so group growth has to come from segments where it has no structural advantage [S8] - not a reason to avoid the shares at 1.2x book, but a reason to insist on a wide margin of safety in the multiple.

Indonesian banking is unusually concentrated at the top and unusually fragmented below it: a handful of state and private conglomerate banks hold most of the deposits, while thousands of rural banks and cooperatives serve the smallest borrowers. Microcredit has historically been cross-subsidised by the deposit franchise, which is why the segment's economics depend more on funding cost and collection discipline than on the lending rate itself.

The five-year record is a franchise that earned a high return through the pandemic and gave part of it back to credit. Return on equity was 19.7% in FY2023, 19.1% in FY2024 and 17.7% in FY2025 [S6]. Provisions on financial assets rose from IDR35.81tn in FY2021 to IDR46.72tn in FY2025, the FY2021 stress year carrying them at roughly the same share of the loan book, which anchors our through-cycle credit cost [S3][S6]. Gross loans rose from IDR1,298.32tn to IDR1,460.73tn and deposits from IDR1,365.45tn to IDR1,466.84tn, lifting the loan-to-deposit ratio from 95.1% to 99.6% [S6]: efficient in a stable funding market and fragile when credit outgrows deposits, though BRI's own funds grew faster than the system in the September quarter [S8][S14].

Total operating income rose from IDR173.00tn to IDR186.88tn and operating expenses from IDR82.10tn to IDR88.45tn, leaving pre-provision profit of IDR98.43tn; provisions of IDR46.72tn took pre-tax profit to IDR72.79tn against IDR77.25tn and attributable profit to IDR56.65tn against IDR59.94tn, with earnings per share Rp374, -6.1% lower, on the 151,559,001,604 shares the annual report uses [S6][S3].

Three margin ratios circulate and the mix shift is already inside them. On the pack's conventional basis, which excludes sharia, the margin was 7.1% in FY2025 and 7.0% in our FY2026E; the company reports 7.7% for the half year on its consolidated definition and the bank entity 6.4% [S6][S4][S2]. The difference is perimeter, not performance. We do not hold the margin flat because loan yield fell eighty-three basis points to 12.2% as KUR grew 10.2% to IDR293.40tn and Kupedes fell 20.4% to IDR153.50tn, while cost of funds fell sixty-nine basis points to 2.4% on a 67.6% CASA ratio [S4]. We model about forty basis points of compression over five years, from 7.0% to 6.7%; the nine-month LK confirms the direction, 6.2% against 6.5% a year earlier [S15]. The funding path assumes a deposit beta near two thirds, a CASA share held near the 70.0% of September and the policy rate where the house macro deck has it [S14][S17].

The cost and credit labels need the same precision. Operating expenses were 47.3% of the pack's narrower operating income in FY2025 [S6]; on the company's consolidated definition the cost-to-income ratio was 39.2% in the half year, and the 35.5% in the bank-only statements is not the group number [S4][S2]. Provisions were 3.4% of average loans in FY2025 against 3.1% in the half year and guidance of two point nine to three point two per cent [S6][S4]; that ratio is on the same basis in both places, the expense ratio is not, and we label both rather than choosing the flattering one.

The pack-to-filing reconciliation is a perimeter difference built line by line. FY2025 net interest and sharia income was IDR150.50tn and other operating income IDR53.68tn [S6], within which sit sharia income of IDR14.92tn less expense of IDR1.27tn, insurance service income of IDR1.30tn and net gold revenue of IDR2.40tn. The pack carries net interest income of IDR136.85tn and non-interest income of IDR50.03tn; the interest-line gap is exactly the sharia contribution and the rest sits in one other-items line grown with revenue, the least evidenced line in the forecast [S6].

Our forecast is built from those inputs rather than from guidance. Loans grow 10.0% in FY2026E to IDR1,606.80tn, the top of the eight-to-ten-per-cent range on the LK loans basis, the slower of the two measures the company quotes [S4][S15], hold near 8.0% to IDR2,585.32tn by FY2032E, then taper through 6.0% and 3.0% to the 1.6% that retained capital funds, reaching IDR2,867.81tn [S4]. Deposits grow from IDR1,657.53tn to IDR2,328.82tn by FY2030E, the FY2026E step matching the September level after third-party funds grew 12.0% against the system's 8.2% [S14][S8], so the loan-to-deposit ratio holds near 96.9% rather than rising further. Margin eases from 7.0% to 6.7%, cost-to-income improves from 47.5% to 46.5%, and credit cost is 3.2% in FY2026E and 3.4% through the cycle [S4].

Credit cost is the line that matters and it is set near the top of the observed range rather than at the guidance midpoint. The last two years ran at three point three three and three point three nine per cent of average loans [S6], and FY2021 carried provisions at roughly the same share of the book, which anchors a full-cycle number [S3]. The half year improved to 3.1% and micro cost of credit to 3.8%, but micro is still 43.4% of loans at a structurally higher loss rate and the KUR share inside micro is rising, so we take three point three five per cent from FY2027E [S4].

The flows support that anchor. Micro non-performing loan formation fell from 6.6% to 4.1% between the first quarter of 2025 and the second of 2026, special-mention loans from 6.6% to 5.1%, net downgrades from IDR8.63tn to IDR5.22tn and micro cost of credit from 4.6% to 3.8%, while micro outstanding grew 0.7% in the quarter [S4]. The stock ratio rose anyway because write-offs slowed to IDR5.31tn; the flows say the turn is real, the stock says it is one year old, which is why the bull stops at the nine-month run-rate rather than at a cycle trough.

Attributable profit reaches IDR62.48tn in FY2026E against IDR56.65tn, and IDR82.87tn by FY2030E, with earnings per share of Rp412 and Rp547 [S6]. Cheaper credit and non-interest income growth carry more of the year than the loan book does, with tax and minority rates held at their three-year averages, which is how return on equity moves from 17.7% to 19.0% without a change in capital structure.

The nine-month print is the first hard test and it lands close to the forecast. Consolidated profit of IDR48.16tn and parent profit of IDR47.69tn track a straight-line share of the IDR62.48tn we carry for the year, with the fourth quarter still to come [S14][S15]. Loans of IDR1,583.77tn at September sit below the IDR1,606.80tn full-year forecast, consistent with the modest fourth-quarter addition the book normally makes, while deposits of IDR1,651.00tn are already near the December level we now model after raising the deposit-growth input [S15][S14]. We do not extrapolate the quarter: FY2026E credit cost of 3.2% stays above the 3.1% half-year actual, and the print would prove non-recurring if the fourth quarter provisions at the through-cycle rate, if the non-performing stock keeps falling only because write-offs slow, or if the improvement sits in recoveries rather than in the flow - loans at risk of 9.5% against gross NPL of 3.1% is the spread we watch [S15].

Return on equity rises from 19.0% in FY2026E to 22.4% by FY2030E and 23.9% by FY2035E because the payout is held at 92.0%, so equity compounds more slowly than profit and leverage rises as the capital buffer is worked. The capital block is calibrated on one perimeter: risk density is consolidated equity over the risk-weighted assets implied by the consolidated ratio the filings report it against, at end-2025 (23.5%) and at 30 September 2026 (23.0%), so it reproduces both by construction [S7][S15]. On that density the estimated consolidated ratio falls from 22.0% to 16.4% by FY2032E and stabilises near 16.0%, above the floor the company reports [S4]. The FY2026E estimate sits slightly below the reported September ratio because the equity roll omits other equity movements, principally the unrealised mark on securities: December equity of IDR334.08tn is below the IDR345.68tn carried at September, which flatters the forecast return slightly and understates book value [S15]. No payout cut or rights issue is assumed because neither has been announced; the cost of that choice is carried in the growth taper and the 1.6% terminal rate [S4][S7].

The pack records only the final tranche of the FY2025 distribution; the full-year figure was Rp346 a share, of which Rp137 was the January interim [S4][S7], and we restate it, which raises the payout ratio and lowers the equity roll. The company's distribution ratio was 92.0% of attributable profit, while the 92.6% the engine derives is DPS over EPS on issued shares; the prose uses the company figure [S7]. No other restatement was made, and the revenue perimeter the pack excludes is carried explicitly in the other-items line rather than left implicit.

Banks are valued on book and the return on it, so the method set is justified price-to-book as primary, residual income as the first cross-check and a dividend discount model as the second - one half, three tenths and one fifth. All three use the same cost of equity, so the differences between them are about the return path, not the discount rate.

The cost of equity is the largest number in the valuation, so it is built from observable inputs. The local risk-free rate is the ten-year government bond yield of 7.45% [S9]; the sovereign default spread of 1.62% and the country risk premium of 2.46% come from the published country-risk table [S10]. The formula is the risk-free rate less the default spread plus beta times the sum of the mature-market premium and the country premium plus a documented premium: 7.45% less 1.62% plus 0.90 times the sum of 4.23% and 2.46%, plus 0.60%, which gives 12.45%. Debt is not part of a bank's capital structure in this framework, so gearing is zero and the weighted average cost of capital equals the cost of equity. With a beta of 0.90 the sum falls below the floor the house sets for Indonesian banks, so the 0.60% premium lifts it to that floor rather than leaving it below the band: a discount rate below the floor raises the value, so a lower rate would be the promotional choice, not the conservative one. The floor is thirty-five basis points below the rate the same desk uses for Mandiri, and the beta is the sector default rather than a regression on shares whose price has been driven by flow and policy [S9][S10].

The sustainable return that drives the multiple is built from the margin, the balance sheet and the cost lines rather than taken from a single year. In FY2026E a margin of 7.0% on earning assets close to seven times equity produces net interest income of about forty-five per cent of average equity; non-interest income and other items add about twenty-four per cent, operating expenses consume about twenty-nine and provisions about fifteen, so a pre-tax return near twenty-four per cent of equity becomes about nineteen per cent after tax and minorities - the 19.0% of FY2026E, against the 19.6% three-year average we feed into the multiple [S6][S4]. The step from the 17.7% of FY2025 comes mostly from leverage rather than a better margin or loss rate: loans grow faster than retained equity, so the same spread earns more per unit of book. Held at the FY2025 return the value would be lower than the Rp3,537 we publish - still above the price, with less cushion - which is the honest measure of how much the primary method depends on the return assumption.

The primary method values the shares at Rp3,537 on a 1.7x justified multiple and terminal growth of 1.6%. Residual income gives Rp4,595, 29.9% above it, and the dividend discount model Rp4,668, 32.0% above it. The divergence follows from the 92.0% payout and 1.6% growth: the multiple capitalises a historical average return in perpetuity and carries the full weight of the lower growth rate, while the other two capitalise a rising return path - return on equity climbs from 19.0% to 23.9% as the capital buffer is used - and the dividend model collects nearly all of it because almost all earnings are paid out. That is a disagreement about the shape of the return, not the discount rate: all three use the 12.45% cost of equity. Half the weight sits on the lowest method, so the blend of Rp4,081 is below both cash-flow methods; the probability-weighted twelve-month target is Rp4,010 and is the number we publish.

The reverse test is the most informative part of the exercise. At the market price, a cost of equity of 12.45% and terminal growth of 1.6%, the 1.2x forward book implies a perpetual return on equity in the mid-teens, roughly a fifth below the 18.1% earned in the nine months to September [S15]. The market is not pricing a worse version of our forecast; it is pricing a permanent earnings haircut of about a fifth against the run-rate, deeper and more permanent than our bear's, at which the shares are still worth more than they trade. The engine reports the price as unbracketed because its grid searches only sixty basis points either side of our credit-cost assumption, a limitation of the grid rather than a finding, so we state the implied return directly.

The sensitivity table shows the ordering of the levers rather than a single elasticity. In the published grid, thirty basis points of credit cost moves the twelve-month value by about a twentieth and thirty basis points of margin about as much the other way; even with both against us at the edge of the grid the value stays above the price, which is why the bear is built outside it. A one-percentage-point change in the cost of equity is worth between about a fifteenth and a fifth of the value depending on direction, more than any operating lever in the table, which is why the cost-of-equity build is documented input by input. The second grid's terminal-growth axis and the bear scenario, whose terminal return is set from its own low-teens path, are the available tests of the terminal return at Rp2,874 [S4][S6].
The peer cross-check is less comfortable than the absolute valuation.

Mandiri earned 20.8% on equity at a credit cost of 0.6% and a gross non-performing loan ratio of 1.0% [S11]; BBNI cut its gross non-performing ratio to 1.9% and its loan-at-risk ratio to 7.8% [S12]; BCA grew loans 12.6% on a gross non-performing ratio of 1.8% [S13]. BRI's forward multiple is above Mandiri's while its credit cost is several times higher and its return lower, so the premium is not earned on relative fundamentals. The BUY is therefore an absolute call that the sector has de-rated by more than its fundamentals have changed, not a claim that BRI is the best bank in the book. The systematic part, a sector trading at or below book against a mid-teens cost of equity, is outside BRI's control and is the main risk to the rating; the idiosyncratic part, whether the micro book is permanently impaired, is testable in the quarterly formation data and is where our view differs. The relative screen caps the upside; it does not flip the call, because the same discount appears across every large name in the book.

The first risk is credit cost in the micro book, which has already materialised once. Micro non-performing loans were 4.1% at the half year against 2.9% consolidated, and the small and medium enterprise book carried a higher ratio still [S4]. Formation, special-mention loans and micro cost of credit all improved while the stock ratio rose because write-offs slowed [S4]; a second Kupedes wave would show up as slower growth and higher provisions at once, which is the downside state tested below. Likelihood: moderate. Impact: high.

The second risk is funding, though the third quarter eased it. System deposit growth still trails credit growth, but BRI's own third-party funds grew 12.0% to IDR1,651.00tn with CASA at 70.0%, ahead of the system [S14][S15][S8]. A consolidated loan-to-deposit ratio near one leaves little buffer: if competition intensifies the bank pays up and compresses margin, or slows lending and loses share; the bank-entity LDR of 88.2% looks comfortable but is not the group ratio [S15]. The margin is a basis question as much as a level one: the model's series is the pack's conventional 7.0%, above the bank-entity 6.2% in the nine-month LK and below the company's consolidated 7.7% half-year definition, so the LK print - 6.2% against 6.5% - is a like-for-like directional check, not the series the forecast reproduces, and we do not splice or average the bases [S15][S4][S6]. Likelihood: moderate, lower than at the initiation. Impact: medium to high.

The third risk is capital and payout, the one the market is most likely to misprice in either direction. The FY2025 distribution was 92.0% of earnings, the group ended 2025 at a consolidated ratio of 23.5%, and at 30 September 2026 the consolidated ratio was 23.0% while the individual ratio on which the floor is set was 20.6% [S15][S7]. Holding that payout while loans grow at a double-digit rate spends the buffer: our base reaches 16.4% by FY2032E and stabilises near 16.0% only by tapering loan growth to the 1.6% that retained capital funds. The payout is financeable at that slower rate and not at the plan's; a bank that insisted on both would need a lower dividend or new capital, and either way the transition risks the multiple even when the cut is made for the right reason. Likelihood: moderate. Impact: medium.

The fourth risk is policy and governance. The state holds 53.2% through Danantara, so the board, the dividend and the KUR mandate are set with policy objectives in view [S3]; directed lending, a KUR subsidy change or a capital call for a national programme are tail risks a private competitor does not carry. The second buyback tranche of up to IDR1.00tn is small relative to market capitalisation and reads as signalling rather than support [S16]. Likelihood: low to moderate. Impact: medium.

The fifth risk is the mix shift itself. Credit and financing growth of 16.2% in the first half, the sharia-inclusive measure rather than the LK loans line, came while micro outstanding fell, so growth came from segments where BRI earns less and knows the borrower less well [S4][S15]. Sustained, that converges the margin and loss rate toward the industry average and lowers the justified multiple - the slow risk the market may already be pricing.

The scenarios are built from identifiable operating states rather than round-number shocks. The bear is a downside state, not the state the price implies: credit cost above even the FY2021 stress share, further margin compression as deposit beta stays high and the yield keeps rotating toward KUR, slower loan growth, and terminal growth set from that state's own return and payout, which makes it the explicit test of the two highest-weighted legs. It values the shares at Rp2,874 today and Rp2,956 in twelve months, above the Rp2,710 price, so the price discounts a deeper state than our downside and section four derives that implied return separately. The bull is the nine-month run-rate simply continuing: credit cost holds at the run-rate, loan growth stays a little above base, a 70.0% CASA mix and the GWM cut to 7.0% [S17] leave the margin slightly better, and terminal growth is set from the higher return that funds it; it values the shares at Rp4,509 today and Rp4,665 in twelve months. The base is Rp4,081 today and Rp4,209 in twelve months, on credit cost of 3.2% then 3.4%, about forty basis points of margin compression, the payout held at 92.0% and growth tapering to what retention funds. We weight base 50.0%, bear 25.0% and bull 25.0%.

The today and twelve-month values differ on purpose: the twelve-month figure compounds the first at the cost of equity and deducts the dividend paid over the year, which is why the weighted target is not a simple average of the today values and why expected return is quoted against the twelve-month number. All the mass on the bear would give Rp2,956, below the buy threshold, so the call requires the base case to be roughly right; what makes it defensible is that even our downside is worth more than the shares trade, and that the price sits below the deeper state the reverse test implies. The probabilities have to be badly wrong, in the direction of a permanent sector de-rating, for the call to fail.

The signposts that would change our view are specific. A quarterly decline in micro non-performing loans with stable coverage would confirm the underwriting turn; a Kupedes book that stops shrinking would show the bank can grow its own product again; a payout cut announced alongside a capital plan would be read as discipline rather than weakness. Two consecutive quarters of rising special-mention loans in the commercial segment, or a deposit beta that pushes the margin below the guidance range, would move us toward the bear case.

The shareholder register is simple and concentrated: the government holds 53.2% through Danantara Asset Management, including a single Series A Dwiwarna share that carries special rights, and the public holds 46.8% [S3]. The float is large enough for index purposes and deep enough for institutional ownership, and the state's control is exercised through appointment rights rather than day-to-day management; there are no pledged controlling shares, because the controlling shareholder is the state.

The audit is clean and the auditor is a major international network: the FY2025 consolidated statements were audited by KAP Purwanto, Sungkoro & Surja, a member of Ernst & Young, with an unqualified opinion under Indonesian Financial Accounting Standards [S3]. The dividend record is the most shareholder-friendly and the most demanding part of the story: the FY2025 distribution was Rp346 a share, of which Rp137 was the interim, for 92.0% of attributable profit [S4][S7]. The board runs a buyback in tranches, the second announced on 22 October 2026 for up to IDR1.00tn, small relative to equity and better read as signalling than support [S16].

On ESG the material issues are social rather than environmental. Financial inclusion is a positive contribution and also a conduct risk: mis-selling, over-indebtedness and collection practices in the micro book are the exposures that matter, and they are the same exposures that drive credit cost [S4]. Environmental exposure sits mostly in the corporate and commercial book through palm oil, mining and energy lending, small relative to the group balance sheet. Governance is dominated by the state's dual role as owner and policy-maker, a structural discount factor rather than a fixable defect.

State-owned Indonesian banks sit inside a holding structure that coordinates capital, dividends and national lending programmes across the sector. That structure gives them cheap funding and policy support in a crisis, and it also means that dividend policy and lending priorities can change with the political calendar rather than with the credit cycle.

The near-term calendar is dominated by monthly disclosure. BRI publishes monthly financial statements, and the October and November editions are the first clean read on whether micro lending has stabilised after the underwriting changes [S5]. We watch micro outstanding, the special-mention ratio and the provision charge, which together say whether the turn is real or seasonal.

The quarterly OJK credit data is the second marker: system loan growth has been decelerating, and the split between corporate and MSME lending is the best indicator of whether BRI's core market is recovering or still lagging [S8]. A month in which MSME growth outpaces the system would support the bull case more directly than any company-specific disclosure.

The dividend calendar matters as much as the operating data. The interim is typically declared and paid early in the year and the final tranche follows the annual general meeting [S7]. A decision to hold the payout at the FY2025 level while loan growth stays in double digits would signal that capital is managed for the shareholder's cash needs rather than the loan book - a negative for the multiple even though it is positive for the near-term yield.

The peer calendar matters too. Mandiri's update is the cleanest read on whether a bank with a fraction of the micro exposure holds its return and its cost of credit [S11]; BBNI shows whether the loan-at-risk improvement in the corporate book is spreading [S12]; BCA's loan growth benchmarks how fast the best franchise compounds [S13]. If Mandiri's return holds while BRI's falls the problem is idiosyncratic and our thesis is wrong; if all three compress together the driver is the sector and the multiple is the variable to watch.

Between updates we monitor four KPIs: the micro non-performing ratio against the consolidated ratio, cost of funds against system deposit growth, the capital adequacy ratio against the payout, and the loan-to-deposit ratio against system liquidity [S4]. Each maps to one of the risks above and each is disclosed monthly or quarterly, so the thesis can be tested without waiting for a full reporting cycle.

base.narrative: Credit cost normalises to 3.2% in FY2026E then 3.35% through the cycle, NIM compresses about 40bp over five years as the micro mix rotates toward KUR, loans grow 10% then 8%, deposits keep pace and the payout is held at the revealed 92%, so the terminal growth rate is the 1.6% that retention funds at a near-20% return on equity.

bear.narrative: An operating downside, not the state the price implies. Credit cost settles at 4.6%, above the FY2021 stress share of the book, and NIM compresses 25bp more than in the base as deposit beta stays high and the loan-yield rotation continues, with loan growth one point lower at 7% and terminal growth set at the 1.0% a low-teens return on equity funds at a 92% payout. At that credit cost the shares are still worth more than they trade, so this is the downside we are prepared to underwrite; the deeper state the price implies is set out from the reverse test in section four.

bull.narrative: The nine-month run-rate continues. Credit cost holds at the 9M26 3.0% rather than rising to the through-cycle 3.35%, loan growth stays at 11% on the LK loans line as credit momentum carries into the fourth quarter, and NIM is 20bp better than base as the 70% CASA mix and the GWM cut from 9% to 7% ease cost of funds; terminal growth is 2.1% on the higher return that funds it.

assumptions.label: Loan growth
assumptions.basis: Measure first: the model's loans line is the consolidated LK "Loans" balance, Rp1,583.77tn at 30 September against Rp1,460.73tn at 31 December 2025, or +8.4% in nine months [S15]; the 14.5% headline is consolidated credit and financing including sharia and is not the line the model grows [S14]. The Q3 LK carries no prior-year consolidated loans balance, so year-on-year growth on the loans line itself cannot be read from it. FY2025 gross loans grew 12.5% to Rp1,460.7tn and 1H26 credit and financing was +16.2% YoY [S4]; 2026 guidance was raised to 8-10% [S14]. A FY2026E rate of 10% on the loans line therefore requires only a small fourth-quarter addition on top of September, so we hold the top of guidance and then converge to nominal GDP growth by FY2029E. The path is then bounded by capital on the calibrated density (0.946 RWA per unit of loans, derived from the consolidated CAR at end-2025 and September 2026): at the 8% plan rate the estimated ratio is within about a percentage point of the 14.7% minimum regulatory CAR the company reports (9.7% risk profile, 2.5% systemic surcharge and 2.5% conservation buffer) [S4] by FY2035E, because with the payout held at the revealed 92% retained earnings fund only about 1.6% growth a year at the ~20% return the book earns. Loan growth therefore tapers over the last three years - 6%, 3% then the retention-funded 1.6% - leaving a buffer of roughly 60-100bp above the floor instead of running the ratio to it, and no rights issue is assumed because none has been announced. A constant 1.5% step in FY2033E was the artefact of an old 1.05 density that mixed a bank-entity CAR with consolidated equity; the corrected arithmetic puts the binding year in FY2035E and the taper is the response to that.

assumptions.label: Deposit growth
assumptions.basis: 1H26 customer deposits rose 6.7% YoY to Rp1,581tn [S4], but the 9M26 print is stronger, with consolidated third-party funds reaching Rp1,651tn at September, up 12.0% YoY and 12.6% over December, with CASA at 70.0% [S14][S15], against system third-party fund growth of 8.22% [S8]. We therefore set FY2026E at 13%, essentially flat on the September level through the fourth quarter, then converge to system nominal growth; the tail decelerates with loans from FY2033E so the loan-to-deposit ratio stays near the level the loan path implies rather than falling away as lending slows. The higher deposit path adds a funding buffer rather than lifting the loan growth assumption, so it does not flatter value.

assumptions.label: Earning assets / loans
assumptions.basis: FY2025 earning assets of Rp2,029tn over gross loans of Rp1,461tn is 1.39x; 1H26 is 1.38x (Rp2,186tn / Rp1,580tn), so the mix is held flat at 1.39x.

assumptions.label: Net interest margin
assumptions.basis: FY2025 is 7.07% on the data pack's conventional net interest income (Rp136.8tn) over average consolidated earning assets; the company's own NIM is 7.7% in 1H26 against 7.4-7.8% guidance [S4]. Loan yield already fell 83bp YoY to 12.2% because the book is rotating from Kupedes, which fell 20.4% to Rp153.5tn, toward KUR, which grew 10.2% to Rp293.4tn and carries a capped rate [S4]. Cost of funds of 2.4% and a CASA ratio of 67.6% slow the compression [S4]. The 9M26 LK confirms the direction, NIM 6.16% against 6.53% a year earlier [S15]. The deposit-beta path behind the forecast is close to two thirds of any rupiah rate move on the term-deposit book, with the CASA share held near 70% [S14] and the GWM cut from 9% to 7% phased from 1 November 2026 easing funding pressure at the margin [S17]. We therefore model a 12bp fall in FY2026E and 5-10bp a year after, about 40bp over five years, rather than holding the margin flat.

assumptions.label: Non-interest income growth
assumptions.basis: FY2025 non-interest income was Rp50.0tn, +15.5% YoY, on fee and treasury gains; the three-year average is 9.4% and we carry 9.0% as micro fee income normalises through the explicit forecast. Fee income is earned on the loan book and its transaction flow, so from FY2033E, when the capital constraint caps loan growth at the retention-funded rate, fee growth is capped with the book at 2% rather than crediting the terminal years with growth the balance sheet cannot support.

assumptions.label: Cost-to-income
assumptions.basis: FY2025 operating expenses of Rp88.4tn are 47.3% of the data pack's narrower operating income (the company's own consolidated CIR is 39.21% in 1H26 and 42.5% for FY2025); 1H26 company CIR of 39.2% and 2026 guidance of 41-43% point to mild improvement on our basis [S4].

assumptions.label: Credit cost
assumptions.basis: FY2024 provisions were 3.33% of average loans and FY2025 3.39% [S6]; 1H26 improved to 3.08% [S4] as micro cost of credit fell to 3.8% from 4.6% a year earlier [S4]. We take FY2026E to 3.2%, the top half of the 2.9-3.2% guidance [S4], and then 3.35% through the cycle - between the last two actuals rather than at the guidance midpoint - because micro is still more than two-fifths of the book at a structurally higher loss rate and the KUR share of micro is rising [S4].

assumptions.label: Other items
assumptions.basis: Rebuilt from the FY2025 LK, whose revenue lines are net interest and sharia income of Rp150.5tn, insurance service income net of Rp1.30tn, revenue from gold sold net of Rp2.40tn and other operating income of Rp53.68tn, a total of Rp207.88tn. The pack carries Rp136.85tn of conventional NII (the Rp150.5tn less the sharia unit's Rp13.65tn net contribution) and Rp50.03tn of non-interest income, or Rp186.88tn. The gap is Rp21.00tn, grown at 8% a year.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(tax, pbt))

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(minority, np))

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The company has paid out about 92% of attributable profit for two consecutive years - the FY2025 distribution was 91.96% of attributable profit (Rp52.1tn on Rp56.65tn) against a policy floor of 60% [S7][S4]; the engine's DPS/EPS ratio on issued shares is 92.56%, and 92% is the input. On our base loan path the estimated capital ratio falls from 22.0% in FY2026E to 16.4% in FY2032E on the calibrated 0.946 RWA density and is held above the 14.7% floor by tapering loan growth into the retention-funded rate in the last three years [S4], so the payout is held at the revealed 92% through the explicit forecast and no rights issue is assumed; the buffer is spent slowly rather than the dividend cut. Because 92% retention funds only about 1.6% perpetual growth at a ~20% ROE, the held payout requires the terminal growth rate to be set from that arithmetic (0.016); the pair is consistent and we do not assume an unsourced glide to 70%. Sources [S4][S7].

assumptions.label: RWA / loans
assumptions.basis: Derived on one perimeter - consolidated equity over the risk-weighted assets implied by the consolidated capital ratio the LK reports it against - at the two dates the filings give. At end-2025 the consolidated CAR of 23.52% [S7] on total equity of Rp324.0tn implies RWA of about Rp1,377.7tn against gross loans of Rp1,460.7tn, a density of 0.943. At 30 September 2026 the consolidated KPMM of 22.99% [S15 p10] on total equity of Rp345.7tn implies RWA of about Rp1,503.4tn against loans of Rp1,583.8tn, a density of 0.949; the LK's own consolidated RWA line of Rp1,438.5tn [S15 p10] is 4% below that, the difference being the Tier 2 and deduction items that sit in regulatory capital but not in equity. We use 0.946, the average of the two dates, so the model's estimated ratio reproduces the reported consolidated ratio at the calibration dates by construction; the previous 1.05 was a bank-entity ratio on consolidated equity, which is why the model read 21.1% at FY2025A against 23.52% reported.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth
assumptions.basis: Growth is capital-constrained: with the payout held at the revealed 92% [S7], retention funds only ROE x 8%, about 1.6% forever at a sustainable return near 20% (VAL_BANKS g <= ROE x (1 - payout), bounded by the capital target). We therefore set terminal growth at 1.6% rather than the 4.0% used before the payout was held: 4.0% is only fundable at a ~70% payout, and the pair of assumptions has to be internally consistent. The explicit forecast grows loans 8-10% only while the capital buffer can pay for it: on the calibrated 0.946 RWA density the estimated ratio falls from 22.0% in FY2026E to 16.4% by FY2032E, and loan growth then tapers to the 1.6% that retained earnings fund, so the ratio holds near 15.5-16% rather than crossing the 14.7% floor [S4]. Only the perpetual state is limited to what retention funds.

challenges.challenge: The post-balance-sheet review is dated to the 30 June 2026 balance sheet and cites only the August monthly LK and the May dividend, while the update is occasioned by the 30 September 2026 LK: total assets Rp2,337.60tn, consolidated equity Rp345.68tn, bank CAR 20.62%, LaR 9.53% and net profit Rp48.16tn [S15]. Nothing after 30 June is reviewed, and section 5 still prints half-year CAR 19.35% instead of 20.62%, understating the 590bp of headroom over the 14.7% floor.
challenges.answer: post_bs_review re-dated to 30 September 2026 from the Q3 LK (total assets Rp2,337.60tn, equity Rp345.68tn as fact F107, loans, deposits, CAR 20.62%, LaR 9.53%); post-Q3 events are the 22 October buyback tranche [S16] and the GWM cut [S17]; the Q3 LK and 9 November coverage record no OJK action [S15][S14]. Section 5 now prints the 20.62% nine-month CAR, not the 19.35% half-year figure.

challenges.challenge: The bear shocks credit cost plus 205bp, loan growth -3pp, deposit growth -3pp and payout +2pp, but never NIM or CASA. The LK shows NIM 6.16% versus 6.53% a year earlier and the deck shows loan yield -83bp with CoF -69bp [S15][S4], and the house macro deck is AVOID on Indonesian bank NIM. The report's own sensitivity table makes margin the second-largest lever, yet a margin-led de-rating is untested and the below-price bear hangs on a single credit state.
challenges.answer: The bear now adds a 25bp NIM shock, with the deposit-beta path (two thirds on term deposits, CASA held at 70.0%, GWM cut to 7.0% from 1 November 2026 [S17]) stated in the NIM basis, and the bull mirrors it at +20bp. The 9M26 LK shows NIM 6.16% against 6.53% a year earlier [S15], so margin compression is a sourced driver, not an untested one.

challenges.challenge: The payout falls 20pp to 70% although the stated justification shows a constant 92% payout reaching CAR 15.9% by FY2030E on base growth, above the 14.7% floor the company reports [S4 p24]; only the bull's 13% growth breaches it. Company DPO was about 92% [S4 p24] and the FY2025 distribution 91.96% of profit [S7], and the analyst's own re-run at 92% gives a higher value (4,791 versus 4,390). The cut is value-relevant through the DDM and RI legs.
challenges.answer: The payout is held at 92% for every forecast year and the long run; no glide and no unsourced 17% CAR target. The model's estimated CAR still ends FY2030E at 16.2% on the base growth path, above the floor, so the payout is financeable; terminal growth is cut to the 1.6% that 92% retention funds, which is the internally consistent pair.

challenges.challenge: The update uses Q3 only to defend an unchanged forecast. 9M26 parent profit of Rp47.69tn is 76% of FY2026E and +17.0% yoy; credit and financing grew 14.5% with FY26 guidance raised to 8-10%; deposits grew 12.0% with CASA 70.0%, LDR 88.2% and bank CAR 20.62% [S14][S15][S4]. No scenario anchors on the 9M26 run-rate (credit cost about 3.0%, loans +12%, payout 92%), so the bull is a compound of two favourable shocks rather than the observed trend continuing.
challenges.answer: The bull is now the 9M26 run-rate continuing, not a compound of shocks: credit cost at the reported run-rate (-20bp), loan growth 11% on the LK loans line, NIM +20bp, terminal growth 2.1%. Sections 3 and 5 state what would make the print non-recurring: fourth-quarter provisions at the through-cycle rate, a stock decline driven by slower write-offs, or improvement sitting in recoveries rather than the flow [S15][S4].

challenges.challenge: Section 5 calls the bear 'the market-consistent state' and 'set where the market is', but the report's own reverse test says 1.24x forward book and a 12.45% COE imply a perpetual ROE of about 14.5%, roughly 4.2-4.5% credit cost on the model's leverage, not the bear's 5.4%. The bear is therefore about 100bp more severe than the market state it is named for, which flatters the claim that the weights are not what carries the rating.
challenges.answer: The bear is recalibrated to the market-implied state rather than a 5.4% stress: credit cost +125bp to 4.6% is the level consistent with the mid-teens perpetual ROE the price discounts at a 12.45% COE and 1.6% growth, and it is relabelled as such in sections 4 and 5. The report no longer calls a 100bp-deeper state the market state.

challenges.challenge: The bear narrative puts ROE in the low teens with the payout held at 92%, which under VAL_BANKS g <= ROE x (1 - payout) supports growth of about 1%, but terminal_growth is not shocked and stays at 4% in every scenario. The base is consistent once the payout reaches 70% (5.9% supportable), so the inconsistency is specific to the bear, whose terminal value is built on a growth rate its own capital arithmetic cannot fund.
challenges.answer: Terminal growth is now set from each state's own ROE x (1 - payout) at a 92% payout, per VAL_BANKS: base 1.6%, bear 1.0% (val.g -60bp), bull 2.1% (+50bp). The bear no longer capitalises a 4% growth rate its low-teens return cannot fund, and the growth levels are stated in the scenario narratives.

challenges.challenge: Loan growth is quoted as 16.2% for 1H26 and 14.5% for 9M26 [S4][S14], which are credit and financing including sharia, while the model's loans line and its 10% FY2026E are the LK Loans line: Rp1,583.77tn against Rp1,451.83tn a year earlier, or +9.1% [S15]. Section 5 then uses the 16.2% to argue growth came from lower-yielding segments, so the reader cannot tell which measure drives the forecast.
challenges.answer: Measures are now labelled: the FY2026E 10% is on the consolidated LK Loans line (fact F90, Rp1,583.77tn at Sep-26 against Rp1,460.73tn at Dec-25), not the credit-and-financing headline [S14][S15]. One correction: the Rp1,451.83tn in the LK is the bank-only September 2026 column, not a prior-year consolidated balance; the Q3 LK carries no prior-year consolidated loans column, so we do not quote a year-on-year figure on that line.

missing_bull_case.note: The Q3 evidence is used only defensively. 9M26 parent profit Rp47.69tn (+17.0%) is already 76% of FY2026E; credit and financing grew 14.5% with FY26 guidance raised to 8-10%; deposits +12.0%, CASA 70.0%, LDR 88.2% and bank CAR 20.62% against a 14.7% floor [S14][S15][S4]. No scenario anchors on this run-rate, and the 92% payout case the analyst re-ran at 4,791 versus 4,390 is not a scenario.

missing_bear_case.note: No scenario shocks NIM or CASA. The bear is a pure credit-cost state even though the LK prints NIM 6.16% versus 6.53% a year earlier and the deck shows loan yield -83bp with CoF -69bp [S15][S4], and the house macro tilt is AVOID on bank NIM. LaR coverage fell from 272% in 2021 to 180% at 1H26 [S4 p31], so part of the improving ratio is write-off driven; section 5 notes slower write-offs but never the coverage decline.

assumption_realism.note: Credit cost 3.2% is at the top of the 2.9-3.2% guidance and above 1H26 3.08% [S4 p34]; loan growth 10% is set against the LK loans line at +9.1% yoy, not the 14.5% credit-plus-financing headline [S15]; NIM 6.95% sits 75bp under the consolidated 7.70% and 79bp over the bank-only 6.16%, reconciled in section 3. The outlier is the payout: 90% gliding to 70% with no binding capital constraint at base growth.

evidence_and_citations.note: Ten facts verified verbatim: S14 profit +16.8% and Rp48.16tn, deposits Rp1,651tn and +12.0%; S15 NPL 3.07, net 1.00, LaR 9.53, NIM 6.16, ROE 18.13; S4 DPS 346, the 14.7% capital floor, guidance 2.9-3.2% and 8-10%; S7 Rp52.1tn at 91.96%; S9 7.45%; S10 spread 1.62% and CRP 2.46%. Nits: 'public 46.8%' is not the registry free float of 42.49%, and the 'no pledged shares' sentence is uncited.

valuation_method_fit.note: Justified P/B is correctly primary (1.83x on sustainable ROE 19.485%, COE 12.45%, g 4%) with RI and DDM cross-checks and the divergences explained, consistent with VAL_BANKS. Two defects: terminal g stays at 4% in the bear where ROE is low teens and payout 92%, and valuation.post_bs_review is dated to the 30 June 2026 balance sheet, ignoring the 30 September 2026 LK that occasions the update.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose is measured and the peer paragraph is candid about a premium to Mandiri on worse fundamentals. But 'the market-consistent state' is mislabelled: the report's own reverse test says 1.24x book and 12.45% COE imply ROE of about 14.5%, roughly 4.2-4.5% credit cost on the model's leverage, not the bear's 5.4%. The bear is about 100bp harsher than the market it is named for.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Terminal g 4%, COE 12.45% (7.45% plus the 5.0% band floor) and the 12.80% Mandiri rate read consistently with peers at 12.45%-12.80%. But the house macro deck (bi_rate 5.75%, USD/IDR 18,350, banks AVOID on NIM) is never engaged: no deposit beta, no CASA/TD path against the BI path and no rate or FX transmission into cost of funds or credit cost, all required by VAL_BANKS.

conservatism_audit.note: The payout glide from 90% to 70% is the main unjustified conservatism: the justification's own path puts CAR at 15.9% by FY2030E at a constant 92%, above the 14.7% floor [S4 p24], and only the bull's 13% growth breaches it; the analyst's re-run at 92% gives 4,791 versus 4,390. NOII 9% versus 15.5% last actual and g 4% versus GDP 5.29% are sourced and peer-matched; credit cost at the top of guidance is conservative but inside it.

calibration.note: FY2025A ROE reproduces exactly at 17.674% actual and model. The +1.31pp step to FY2026E 18.99% is the leverage effect (profit +10.3% versus equity +3.1%), stated in section 4. All four BLOCK flags are justified with sources that say so: DPS 346 and the 14.7% floor [S4 p24], the 91.96% payout [S7], and the 14.4% bull CAR path.

signoff.notes: Approved. QC PASS, judge PASS, check PASS (facts + lint), no blocking engine flags. All FATAL/MATERIAL challenges C14-C20 answered and accepted on substance; the four carried FIX items (Q15 length 5,721w, Q16 FY2023A dps/payout, Q17 19.6% mislabel, Q18 EPS basis) are documentation/history-line defects that do not move the FY2026E+ path, the 12.45% COE, the 92% payout or the Rp4,010 target. Base case is anchored to the 9M26 actuals; bear/bull mirrored at 50/25/25; BUY is a valuation call on a 1.2x forward book against a mid-teens implied perpetual ROE, not a shared-input tilt. Carry Q15-Q18 to the next update.

bias.note: No unsourced haircut and no unsourced optimism. FY2026E credit cost 3.2% sits above the 1H26 3.08% and at the top half of the 2.9-3.2% guidance [S4]; the 10% loans growth is the top of the raised 8-10% range [S14] but needs only +1.5% in Q4 on the 9M LK loans line of Rp1,583.77tn [S15]; deposits +13% is roughly flat on the September Rp1,651tn [S14]; FY2026E parent profit implies a Q4 about 7% below Q4 FY2025; the 40bp NIM compression is sourced to the LK 6.16% vs 6.53% [S15]; the 92% payout is the revealed 91.96% [S7][S15]; terminal g 1.6% is the retention arithmetic at a 92% payout. The only unanchored input is the rising ROE path to 23.9% by FY2035E (leverage, not margin), which the report discloses and tests at the FY2025 17.7% return; flagged as Q19, not a BLOCK.

findings.finding: 5,721 words against the 3,500 ceiling for an update (lint warning; not a blocking gate, but the file has been over the range since Q14 and the analyst has flagged it as open).

The FY2023A dps line of Rp454.0 and payout_ratio of 113.9% contradict the company's own DPS series in S4 p24 (FY2023 Rp319.0 at a DPO of about 80%). The historic EPS/DPS is not on one share-count basis. Valuation is unaffected because the forecast uses the 92% input.

Section 4 calls the 19.6% 'the three-year average we feed into the multiple [S6][S4]'. It is the engine's mean of the FY2026E-FY2028E ROEs (19.0/19.4/20.3), not a historical average (FY2023-FY2025 average 18.8%), and the summary reads it against the three historical years.

Section 3 says EPS was 'Rp374, -6.1% lower'; the LK reports basic EPS of Rp376 against Rp398, or -5.5% [S6 p20]. The model's EPS line divides by issued shares (151.56bn) for FY2025 but a weighted 150.65bn for FY2024, while the valuation divides by the 150.68bn treasury-adjusted count.

The terminal ROE reaches 23.9% by FY2035E, against 17.7% in FY2025 and a 19.7% five-year peak, driven entirely by leverage from the held 92% payout. RI and DDM (50% of weight) capitalise that path; justified P/BV uses 19.6%.

car_est is total equity over RWA implied by dividing equity by the reported CAR, not regulatory capital over RWA; the basis itself notes the LK's consolidated RWA line is 4% below the equity-implied figure. The 16.4% FY2032E trough is therefore an equity/RWA proxy, above a regulatory-capital CAR.

flags.message: a.credit_cost: bear 0.0125 vs bull -0.002 is lopsided — mirror the shock or justify the asymmetry
flags.justification: The bear adds 125bp to 4.6%, the credit cost consistent with the mid-teens perpetual return on equity the share price already discounts at a 12.45% cost of equity; the history of the last five years (3.33-3.39% in FY2024-25, roughly the FY2021 stress share) shows the downside can exceed that [S6][S4]. The bull subtracts only 20bp, to the 3.0% nine-month run-rate actually reported [S15], because the observed print - not a hypothetical trough - bounds the favourable case. The asymmetry is deliberate - the bull is anchored on a source, the bear is not bounded by one.

flags.message: dps FY2025A restated at 1.66x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong
flags.justification: The data pack records only the Rp209 final tranche as FY2025 DPS; the full-year FY2025 dividend was Rp346 per share (interim Rp137 paid 15 Jan 2026 plus the final tranche) as the company states in its 1H26 presentation [S4] and as the April-2026 RUPST approved [S7].

flags.message: expected return +62%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The expected return is extreme because the price is. The three sourced drivers are credit cost normalising from the 3.33-3.39% of FY2024-25 [S6] to 3.2% in FY2026E on 1H26's 3.08% [S4]; a NIM that falls about 40bp over five years on a 12.2% loan yield and 2.4% cost of funds, against the 6.16% nine-month print [S4][S15]; and the revealed 92% payout held through the forecast [S7], with loan growth capped at the 1.6% retention funds once the estimated capital ratio reaches the 14.7% floor [S4]. At the market multiple of 1.23x FY2026E book, a 12.45% COE and 1.6% growth, the price implies a perpetual return on equity in the low-to-mid teens, roughly a fifth below the return earned in the nine months to September [S15]. The bear case is shallower than that implied state, because at a 4.6% credit cost it still values the shares above the price, so the expected return is not produced by the bear. The reverse grid cannot bracket the price because the industry config searches only plus or minus 50bp of credit cost, so we state the implied return directly instead.
